To estimate the causal effect of home broadband access on 11th-grade standardized test scores, I will use a two-stage least squares (2SLS) design restricted to the 104 phase-3 school districts. The instrumental variable is `crew_order`, which reflects the randomized lottery order determining when the fiber construction crew arrived in each phase-3 district. Although `fiber_phase` was also randomized by lottery, it violates the exclusion restriction because it concurrently funded new school computer labs at phase onset. In contrast, `crew_order` exogenously shifted the timing of household broadband deployment without altering the timing of computer lab grants or phase assignment. The first stage regresses district household broadband subscription share on `crew_order` and baseline district controls (such as `median_income`, `rural_share`, `per_pupil`, `college_share`, and `enroll`). The second stage estimates the impact of instrumented broadband adoption on district average 11th-grade test scores.

We will estimate the causal effect of home broadband access on 11th-grade test scores using an instrumental variables design restricted to the 104 phase-3 school districts. The treatment is the district share of households with a broadband subscription, the outcome is the district average 11th-grade test score, and the instrument is `crew_order`, the lottery-assigned construction crew arrival month. Although `fiber_phase` was also assigned by lottery across the full sample, it violates the exclusion restriction because phase assignment determined when districts joined the connected list and began receiving annual state school technology funding for laptops and labs. In contrast, all phase-3 districts entered the connected list simultaneously, so `crew_order` shifts home broadband timing without altering school technology funding. Baseline district characteristics such as `median_income`, `rural_share`, and `per_pupil` spending can be controlled for to improve precision. The primary threat is reduced statistical power and potential weak instrument concerns given the smaller sample of 104 districts.

We will estimate the causal effect of home broadband access on 11th-grade standardized test scores using an instrumental variables (2SLS) strategy restricted to the 104 Phase 3 school districts. While the overall lottery phase (`fiber_phase`) violates the exclusion restriction because it simultaneously funded new school computer labs at phase onset, the within-phase construction timing (`crew_order`) was randomly assigned via lottery and affected only the timing of fiber arrival. All Phase 3 districts received their computer lab grant at the same time, ensuring that variations in `crew_order` affect student outcomes exclusively through the timing of last-mile residential broadband availability. In the first stage, we instrument the district's household broadband subscription rate with `crew_order`, which decreases subscription share by 1.0 percentage point per month of delay. The outcome is the district's average 11th-grade test score, and we control for baseline covariates including `median_income`, `rural_share`, `per_pupil`, and `enroll`. The primary threat to validity is limited statistical power given the smaller sample of 104 districts, alongside potential violations if earlier crew arrivals directly affected school network connectivity before private home take-up.

We will implement a two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental variables strategy exploiting the randomized timing of the state's subsidized fiber backbone rollout. The instrument is `fiber_phase`, which reflects the 2010 lottery assignment of eligible districts into four sequential construction phases. The first stage estimates the effect of `fiber_phase` on the endogenous treatment, the district share of households with a broadband subscription. The second stage estimates the causal effect of household broadband access on the district average 11th-grade standardized test score. Baseline covariates—such as `median_income`, `rural_share`, `per_pupil`, `college_share`, and `enroll`—will be included to assess balance from the lottery and improve precision. The primary threat to identification is a violation of the exclusion restriction if earlier fiber backbone arrival directly influenced educational outcomes through non-household channels, such as direct fiber connections to school administrative facilities or concurrent commercial spillovers.

To estimate the causal effect of home broadband access on 11th-grade test scores, we use an instrumental variables (IV) design restricted to the subsample of 104 phase-3 school districts. The instrument is `crew_order`, which reflects the randomized lottery order (0 to 11 months) governing when construction crews arrived to install fiber. The endogenous treatment is the district's household broadband subscription share, and the outcome is the district average 11th-grade standardized test score. This instrument satisfies the exclusion restriction because `crew_order` affected solely the timing of local fiber installation, whereas all phase-3 districts were placed on the connected list and entered into the state digital-readiness register simultaneously at the start of phase 3. By contrast, using overall phase assignment (`fiber_phase`) would violate the exclusion restriction because earlier phases received additional years of school technology funding for laptops and computer labs. The primary threat to validity is limited statistical power due to the restricted sample size of 104 districts, alongside potential violations of the stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA) if infrastructure rollout caused cross-district spillovers.

The lottery assignment makes `fiber_phase` randomly assigned, but it violates the exclusion restriction because the grant simultaneously funded new school computer labs. Using evidence from the independent evaluation that computer labs alone reduced test scores by 0.012 to 0.072 standard deviations per phase delay, we can apply Conley et al. (2012) plausibly exogenous / union of confidence interval bounds. Adjusting the reduced-form estimate (-0.0109) by this direct effect range $[-0.072, -0.012]$ yields point identification bounds of $[-0.0166, -0.0003]$ and a 95% confidence interval of $[-0.0199, 0.0030]$. Because the exclusion restriction is violated and only bounded, no single point estimate is preferred.

We will estimate the causal effect using a two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental variables design restricted to selected adults who returned an application. The endogenous treatment is months enrolled in Medicaid, the outcome is the count of emergency department visits over the following 18 months, and the instrument is `slow_team`. The initial lottery draw (`lottery_selected`) violates the exclusion restriction because selected individuals concurrently received clinic vouchers for free primary-care visits, creating a direct pathway to utilization. In contrast, `slow_team` leverages plausibly exogenous variation in Medicaid enrollment duration generated by random assignment to a caseworker team experiencing six-week approval delays. The empirical specification will control for baseline covariates including prior ED visits, chronic conditions, age, household size, urban status, and language. The primary threat to identification is that caseworker delays could directly alter patients' care-seeking behavior or application persistence through administrative friction rather than solely through the reduction in enrolled months.

INSTRUMENT: slow_team

To estimate the causal effect of Medicaid enrollment duration on emergency department visits, we will use a two-stage least squares instrumental variables design restricted to lottery winners who submitted an application. We instrument the endogenous treatment—months enrolled in Medicaid—using random assignment to the slower caseworker processing team (`slow_team`). While lottery selection (`lottery_selected`) randomized eligibility, it cannot serve as an instrument because selected individuals received free primary care clinic vouchers that directly alter emergency department use regardless of enrollment, violating the exclusion restriction. In contrast, `slow_team` was randomly assigned among applicants and generates exogenous delay, reducing Medicaid enrollment by 2.0 months on average. In addition to the instrument, treatment, and 18-month ED visit outcome, the model will control for baseline characteristics including prior ED visits (`prior_ed`), household size (`hh_size`), chronic conditions (`chronic`), age (`age08`), urban status (`urban`), and language (`english`). The primary threat to this design is that the slow team's delayed processing may have altered final approval or denial rates rather than just timing, potentially violating the exclusion restriction or monotonicity.

We will estimate the causal effect of Medicaid enrollment on emergency department (ED) visits using a two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental variables design restricted to the sample of applicants who submitted an application. The instrument is `slow_team`, an indicator for being randomly routed to the caseworker team with approval delays, which reduces Medicaid enrollment by 2.0 months. We discard `lottery_selected` as an instrument because the state mailed free community primary-care clinic vouchers to all lottery selectees regardless of enrollment status, violating the exclusion restriction. In contrast, random caseworker assignment among applicants satisfies exogeneity and affects subsequent ED visits solely through the duration of Medicaid coverage. The first stage instruments months of Medicaid enrollment with `slow_team`, and the second stage estimates its causal impact on ED visits over the subsequent 18 months. The specification can control for baseline covariates—including `prior_ed`, `age08`, `hh_size`, `chronic`, `urban`, and `english`—to improve estimation efficiency.

While `lottery_selected` is randomized, it violates the exclusion restriction because selected individuals directly received a free primary-care clinic voucher, which can influence ED utilization through a channel other than Medicaid enrollment. We instead exploit `slow_team` as an instrument, restricting the estimation sample to selected individuals who returned an application. Random assignment to the slow caseworker team generated exogenous administrative delays that reduced Medicaid enrollment by an average of 2.0 months, satisfying instrument relevance. Because caseworker routing occurred after application return and merely delayed processing without providing alternative benefits, it plausibly satisfies the independence and exclusion restrictions. In the 2SLS model, we will regress 18-month ED visits on predicted enrollment months while controlling for baseline covariates including prior ED visits, household size, age, and chronic conditions to enhance precision.
